interactions.label: A 45-year-old woman presents with persistent sadness, disturbed sleep, and compl

params.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with persistent sadness, disturbed sleep, and complete loss of interest in activities for 10 days. She has been unable to work during this period. Based on ICD-11 and DSM-5 criteria, why can a major depressive episode NOT be diagnosed at this stage?

answers.text: She does not have enough individual symptoms for the diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The scenario describes depressed mood, sleep disturbance, anhedonia, and occupational impairment — these are characteristic depressive symptoms.

answers.text: Her symptoms have not met the minimum required duration of two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Both ICD-11 and DSM-5 require core symptoms to be present for at least two weeks before a major depressive episode can be diagnosed, even when symptoms are clinically significant.

answers.text: Loss of interest in activities is not considered a core symptom of depression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia) is one of the two anchor symptoms of depression, alongside persistently depressed mood.

answers.text: Functional impairment alone is insufficient; hospitalisation is needed for diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Clinically significant impairment in social or occupational functioning is part of the diagnostic criteria. Hospitalisation is not required.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three requirements for diagnosing a depressive episode: symptoms must persist for at least two weeks, represent a change from previous functioning, and cause significant distress or functional impairment.
Well done. The two-week minimum duration is a key gatekeeper in depression diagnosis — it prevents normal grief and transient low mood from being misclassified as a depressive episode.

interactions.label: Which of the following correctly states the duration criterion for diagnosing a

params.question: Which of the following correctly states the duration criterion for diagnosing a manic episode according to both ICD-11 and DSM-5?

answers.text: Symptoms must persist for at least two weeks, similar to a depressive episode

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The two-week criterion applies to depressive episodes. The duration threshold for mania is shorter — at least one week.

answers.text: Symptoms must be present for at least one week, or any duration if hospitalisation is required

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The hospitalisation exception is clinically important — it recognises that severe mania may require inpatient management before a full week has elapsed.

answers.text: There is no minimum duration criterion; diagnosis rests entirely on symptom severity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A minimum duration of one week is the standard requirement. Only when hospitalisation is required does the duration criterion become unrestricted.

answers.text: Symptoms must last at least 72 hours to differentiate mania from hypomania

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Neither ICD-11 nor DSM-5 uses a 72-hour threshold for manic episodes. The standard criterion is at least one week, with the hospitalisation exception.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key rule: at least one week of persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy — but any duration if the severity requires hospitalisation. Both ICD-11 and DSM-5 encode this exception.
Excellent. Remember to always state both parts of this criterion — the one-week standard and the hospitalisation exception — when discussing mania diagnosis in clinical or examination settings.

params.question: A 32-year-old man presents to your PHC with acute mania — grandiose delusions, pressured speech, reckless spending, and agitation. His family is present. As a primary-care physician, what is your correct approach?

answers.text: Initiate lithium therapy and schedule monthly follow-up to monitor blood levels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Long-term mood stabiliser therapy requires specialist supervision with regular blood-level monitoring. This is beyond the primary-care physician's role in acute mania.

answers.text: Assess immediate safety risks, stabilise acutely, then refer to a psychiatrist

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The three-step framework — Safety, Stabilise, Refer — ensures the patient is bridged safely from crisis to definitive specialist-supervised management of bipolar disorder.

answers.text: Prescribe anxiolytics and discharge with psychoeducation materials for the family

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Anxiolytics alone do not address the underlying manic episode, and discharge without specialist referral leaves the patient at continuing risk of harm.

answers.text: Arrange immediate ambulance transfer without any primary-care intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Safety assessment and acute stabilisation must be performed at the point of first contact. Enlisting the family, removing access to means of harm, and considering the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 are all first-contact responsibilities.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the three-step framework for acute mania at the primary-care level: (1) Safety — assess risks, enlist family, remove means of harm; (2) Stabilise — acute pharmacological management; (3) Refer — the specialist manages bipolar disorder long-term.
Exactly right. In primary care you are the bridge — your job is to keep the patient safe and stabilised until specialist care takes over. Long-term bipolar management is the specialist's domain.
